title: Steel Framing Load Tables: How to Select the Right Studs and Framing System
description: Learn how to use steel framing load tables to choose studs, check design inputs, keep units consistent, and prepare complete, review-ready submittals.
html:
Steel framing load tables help contractors, engineers, architects, and specifiers narrow the available stud and framing options for a project. They organize factors such as product family, wall height, spacing, gauge, loading, and deflection so you can compare compatible members more efficiently.

They do not replace project-specific engineering, code review, or confirmation of the manufacturer’s current design information. The reliable process is to use the table as a selection tool, then verify its assumptions against the actual loads, support conditions, connections, and regulatory requirements.

Quick summary

  • Identify whether the application is non-load-bearing interior framing or structural load-bearing framing.
  • Gather wall height, stud spacing, profile or gauge requirements, support conditions, wind, seismic, and deflection criteria before reading a table.
  • Use the table for the correct manufacturer product family and keep metric or imperial dimensions and loads consistent.
  • Check the selection against current product data, applicable standards, drawings, and project-specific engineering requirements.
  • Send complete project information with your quote or submittal request so the framing selection can be reviewed efficiently.

What Steel Framing Load Tables Show

A steel stud load table is a structured reference for matching a framing member to defined project conditions. Depending on the product and application, it may organize options by stud type, profile, gauge, wall height, spacing, loading condition, orientation, and allowable deflection criterion.

The table is useful only when its assumptions match the proposed installation. A result from one product family, support condition, or design basis should not automatically be transferred to another profile or manufacturer.

Think of the table as a way to narrow the field, not as a standalone approval. The final selection must still be coordinated with drawings, loads, connections, applicable code provisions, and current technical information for the specified product.

Light-Gauge vs. Heavy-Gauge Steel Framing

The first decision is to identify the framing function. Light gauge steel framing is commonly associated with non-load-bearing interior partitions, while heavier structural members may be used where the framing system must resist design loads or support building elements. These categories are not interchangeable simply because both use steel studs.

Decision factorLight-gauge, non-load-bearing framingHeavy-gauge or structural framing
Primary questionCan the partition support its intended finishes and resist applicable service conditions?Can the member and complete system resist specified structural loads and serviceability requirements?
Typical inputsPartition height, spacing, finishes, openings, deflection expectations, and attachment detailsLoads, spans or wall height, spacing, support conditions, bracing, connections, wind, seismic, and deflection
DocumentationProduct data, installation requirements, and the applicable non-load-bearing tableStructural design basis, current load tables, engineering review, connection details, and code coordination

This distinction does not prescribe a member for a particular project. It tells you which product family and technical discussion to begin with. Dass Metal supplies both light- and heavy-gauge steel framing components and supports design and procurement with engineering resources, brochures, and metric and imperial load tables.

Project Inputs to Gather Before Reading a Table

Do not start by choosing a gauge at random. First assemble the information that determines which table applies and whether its assumptions reflect the project.

  • Application: Identify whether the member is for an interior partition, exterior wall, shaftwall, ceiling, infill condition, or structural framing system.
  • Wall height or member span: Record the dimension used by the relevant table, including changes caused by openings, parapets, floor lines, or irregular geometry.
  • Stud spacing: Confirm proposed spacing and whether it changes around openings or special conditions.
  • Profile and gauge: Note the specified product family, profile dimensions, material requirements, and drawing restrictions.
  • Loads: Gather applicable gravity, wind, seismic, impact, cladding, finish, or other project loads.
  • Deflection: Identify the required serviceability limit and the element or finish that controls it.
  • Support and connection conditions: Confirm how the member is supported, braced, fastened, and connected.
  • Location and code basis: Record the project jurisdiction and applicable standard references.
  • Measurement system: Decide whether the design and submittal will use metric or imperial units.

How to Read a Steel Stud Load Table

  1. Confirm the product family. Make sure the table applies to the intended stud, joist, track, or framing component.
  2. Read the design basis and assumptions. Check material properties, loading, support arrangement, orientation, bracing, and deflection criteria.
  3. Match project height and spacing. Find the conditions corresponding to the actual wall height, span, and stud spacing. Do not interpolate unless permitted by the manufacturer or engineer.
  4. Check the governing criterion. Determine whether selection is controlled by strength, deflection, combined loading, stability, or another stated limit.
  5. Verify orientation and connections. Confirm that assumed track arrangement, bracing, fasteners, and supports match the installation.
  6. Record the selection. Capture product name, profile, gauge, spacing, height, units, table reference, assumptions, and engineering notes.

This process prevents treating a single number as the capacity of an entire framing system. Change the product, height, spacing, support, bracing, or loading, and the selection may need review again.

Metric vs. Imperial Steel Framing Tables

Metric and imperial steel framing tables can both be useful, but the project should have one controlled measurement system. Keep dimensions, loads, spacing, deflection limits, and member descriptions internally consistent.

Before issuing a submittal, check that the units in the selected table match the drawings and calculations. If a project must work between systems, document the conversion and have the result verified rather than combining values informally.

How Load Tables Work With Other Technical Documents

Load tables are only one part of a complete technical package. Each document answers a different question:

  • Product brochures and data sheets identify product families, dimensions, material information, accessories, and general applications.
  • Load tables organize member selections under stated design assumptions.
  • Standards and code references establish the applicable design framework.
  • Shop drawings and submittals show intended dimensions, spacing, connections, and coordination.
  • Engineering calculations or review address project-specific responsibility that a general table cannot cover.
  • MSDS or SDS documents provide safety information. They do not establish structural load capacity.

Ontario Code and CSA S136 Context

For structural cold-formed steel work in Ontario, check applicable Building Code provisions with the relevant CSA S136 design basis. Ontario regulatory material identifies CSA S136 in provisions concerning cold-formed steel structures. Review the current Ontario Building Code regulation and other applicable project provisions.

A reference table does not replace confirmation of the current code basis, project loads, design assumptions, and professional review requirements. Projects outside Ontario may follow different governing requirements.

Why Manufacturer-Specific Tables Matter

Steel studs that look similar on a drawing can differ in profile geometry, material properties, thickness, stiffening features, connection requirements, and design assumptions. Those differences can affect performance and table use.

Use the table issued for the product being specified. Do not transfer a result from another manufacturer’s profile, an older project, or an unverified document to a Dass Metal member without confirmation. If the required condition is not represented clearly, ask the manufacturer or project engineer to review it.

This is especially important for custom profiles, unusual wall heights, nonstandard spacing, openings, mixed systems, or demanding wind, seismic, or deflection requirements.

Pre-Quote Checklist for Contractors and Specifiers

Send enough information for the manufacturer or supplier to understand the request without reconstructing the project from incomplete notes. Include:

  • Project name, location, and construction stage.
  • Application and intended framing function.
  • Relevant plans, elevations, sections, specifications, or marked-up details.
  • Wall heights, spans, stud spacing, openings, and support conditions.
  • Required profile, gauge, finish, accessories, and preferred product family.
  • Wind, seismic, gravity, cladding, finish, and other applicable loads.
  • Deflection criteria and connection or bracing requirements.
  • Metric or imperial units for the response and submittal.
  • Estimated quantities, delivery location, required schedule, and phased delivery needs.
  • Applicable code, standard, specification, or engineer’s reference.

A complete request helps distinguish a standard product inquiry from a technical review or custom-profile requirement.

Pre-Submittal Checklist

Before issuing the framing package, verify that the selected member and supporting documents tell the same story.

  • The product name, profile, gauge, and manufacturer match the approved or specified system.
  • Wall height, spacing, orientation, support conditions, and connections match the drawings.
  • The load table reference and design basis are identified.
  • Wind, seismic, strength, and deflection assumptions are stated where applicable.
  • All dimensions, loads, spacing, and deflection values use the intended unit system.
  • Product data, relevant standards, and calculations are included as required.
  • Openings, bracing, clips, tracks, or custom profiles are coordinated.
  • Required engineering or project review is complete.
  • Material quantities and delivery requirements match the latest drawings and schedule.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can a steel framing load table replace a structural engineer’s design?

No. A load table can identify possible members under defined assumptions, but it does not replace project-specific design, code review, connection design, or professional responsibility where required.

Should I use a light-gauge or heavy-gauge steel stud load table?

Start with the framing function. Non-load-bearing partitions and structural systems generally require different product families and selection criteria. Confirm the appropriate table with the drawings, specification, and technical reviewer.

Can metric and imperial load table values be used together?

They should not be mixed informally. Choose the project measurement system and keep dimensions, loads, spacing, deflection limits, and calculations consistent.

What information should I send before requesting guidance?

Provide the application, location, drawings, wall heights, spacing, loads, deflection criteria, support conditions, preferred units, profiles, quantities, schedule, and applicable code references.

Are older CSSBI steel framing load tables still current?

Older reference tables should not automatically be treated as the latest design basis. Confirm current project requirements, applicable Building Code provisions, CSA S136 where relevant, and the manufacturer’s current documentation.

Conclusion: Use the Table to Narrow the Choice, Then Verify the Design

The best way to use steel framing load tables is as part of a coordinated selection workflow. Identify the framing application, gather the height, spacing, loads, deflection, support, connection, code, and unit information, then match those conditions to the manufacturer’s product family.

Do not assume that a table alone establishes suitability. Manufacturer-specific documentation, current standards, project drawings, engineering review, and consistent measurement information all matter before steel studs or related framing components are specified and ordered.
